article.headline: Palantir's Earnings Slide Crowns Four Companies the New AI Elite
article.lede: When Palantir published its Q1 2026 results, it slipped in a competitive benchmark that effectively rewrote the grammar of software valuation — and four names came out on top.
article.body:
The reference in the post is not to some offhand remark by Alex Karp, Palantir's mercurial chief executive, but to a chart embedded in the company's own Q1 2026 investor slides. Palantir, which reported 85% revenue growth and a 60% adjusted operating margin in the quarter, used the occasion to introduce what it called the *Rule of 80 Frontier* — a stricter cousin of the *Rule of 40*, the standard yardstick used to evaluate software companies. The Rule of 40 holds that a healthy tech company's revenue-growth rate plus its operating-margin percentage should sum to at least 40; cross that threshold and the business is, by industry convention, adequately balancing expansion with profitability. Palantir's composite score came in at 145, which is the kind of number that makes venture capitalists check their spreadsheets twice.

The Rule of 80 Frontier, by extension, is simply the cohort of large-cap companies whose combined growth-plus-margin scores exceed 80 — a bar that eliminates most of the S&P 500 in one stroke. According to the slides, five companies cleared it among the top 100 by market capitalisation: Nvidia at 122%, Palantir itself at 94%, Eli Lilly at 89%, Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company at 88%, and Visa at 83%. The poster, Felix Prehn, a former investment banker who runs the Goat Academy retail-investing community, focuses on the top four, noting that all sit above 40 and most crush 80 — a pithy double entendre, since "40" and "80" are also numerical thresholds that technical traders associate with the *Relative Strength Index* (RSI), a momentum oscillator scaled from 0 to 100 that measures the speed and magnitude of recent price moves. In that reading, staying above 40 signals healthy trend momentum, while surging past 80 marks a stock as emphatically overbought by conventional reckoning. Whether Prehn intended both layers simultaneously, or simply borrowed the framing from Karp's slides, the ambiguity is part of the post's charm.

The four companies share a structural trait that goes beyond either metric. Nvidia supplies the hardware substrate for the current AI buildout; TSMC (Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company, the world's dominant contract chipmaker) fabricates the silicon that Nvidia designs; Palantir provides the software layer that turns raw AI inference into operational decisions for governments and corporations; and Eli Lilly's GLP-1 obesity and diabetes drugs represent perhaps the only non-AI sector generating comparable investor excitement right now. Together they form an unintentional coalition of the compounding — businesses where competitive moats are widening at roughly the same pace as revenues.

There is a subtle vanity in Palantir publishing such a list from fourth place on it. The company ranked itself below Nvidia, a business roughly fifteen times its size by revenue. Critics who note that Palantir still derives a meaningful share of income from government surveillance contracts — and who have questioned whether its AI platform, AIP, generates the durable commercial revenue its slides imply — might observe that designing your own peer group is a time-honoured sport in Silicon Valley. Karp, who has described rivals as running software that simply does not work, and once told investors they could find the exit if they disagreed with his politics, is not a man who shies from self-promotion dressed as analysis.

Nevertheless, the underlying numbers are real. Palantir's U.S. commercial revenue grew 133% year-over-year in Q1 2026. Nvidia's data-centre business is approaching $200 billion in annualised revenue. TSMC continues to report record advanced-node utilisation. And Eli Lilly's GLP-1 franchise, led by Mounjaro and Zepbound, has reshaped pharmaceutical revenue expectations globally. That four companies from such disparate corners of the economy — AI silicon, AI software, drug biology — can be meaningfully ranked on the same growth-plus-margin scorecard is itself a data point about how thoroughly the current technology wave has reorganised corporate America's hierarchy of winners.

concepts.definition: A benchmark for software companies: revenue-growth rate (%) plus operating-margin (%) should sum to at least 40. Scores above 40 indicate a healthy balance of growth and profitability; Palantir's Q1 2026 score of 145 was exceptional.

A stricter tier introduced by Palantir in its Q1 2026 earnings slides, identifying large-cap companies whose Rule of 40 composite score exceeds 80. The Q1 2026 list: Nvidia 122%, Palantir 94%, Eli Lilly 89%, TSMC 88%, Visa 83%.

A technical-analysis momentum oscillator scaled from 0 to 100, typically calculated over 14 days. Readings above 70 conventionally signal a stock is overbought; readings above 80 indicate strong upward momentum. The post's 'above 40, most crush 80' phrasing may double as an RSI reading alongside the Rule of 40/80 framing.

article.fact_check: The Rule of 80 Frontier list — Nvidia 122%, Palantir 94%, Eli Lilly 89%, TSMC 88%, Visa 83% — is confirmed by multiple sources citing Palantir's Q1 2026 investor slides published May 4, 2026. Palantir's Rule of 40 score of 145% (85% revenue growth + 60% adjusted operating margin) is confirmed in the company's official earnings release. The tweet's claim that all four named companies are 'above 40' and 'most crush 80' is accurate per those slides. No publicly accessible document was found in which Alex Karp personally narrates a ranked list of companies he admires; the 'Karp list' interpretation that best fits the evidence is the Rule of 80 Frontier chart from Palantir's own Q1 2026 earnings presentation. Felix Prehn is a former investment banker and founder of the Goat Academy retail-finance education community, confirmed by public podcast and website records. The RSI double-reading is plausible but speculative — Prehn's post does not explicitly invoke RSI.

ticker_nvda.name: NVIDIA Corporation
ticker_nvda.blurb: NVIDIA designs graphics processing units (GPUs) and system-on-chip products. Originally a gaming chip company, it became the dominant supplier of AI accelerators — chips that perform the parallel matrix math required to train and run large language models. Its H100, H200, and Blackwell GPU families are the de facto standard for AI training infrastructure at hyperscalers and cloud providers. NVIDIA's CUDA software ecosystem creates deep switching costs: virtually all AI frameworks and models are optimised for CUDA, making competing hardware difficult to adopt at scale. NVIDIA also sells networking (InfiniBand, Ethernet) and data-centre systems.
ticker_nvda.recent: NVIDIA reported FY2026 (ending Jan 2026) revenue of $215.9 billion, up 65% YoY, with data centre revenue reaching $186 billion. The company's forward P/E of ~17.5x on 34.8% projected EPS growth produces a PEG of 0.50 — unusually cheap for what is arguably the most critical infrastructure company in the AI buildout. Hyperscalers (Microsoft, Amazon, Google, Meta) collectively committed over $200 billion in AI infrastructure capex for 2026, the majority flowing through NVIDIA's supply chain.

ticker_pltr.name: Palantir Technologies Inc.
ticker_pltr.blurb: Palantir Technologies, founded in 2003 by Peter Thiel, Alex Karp, and others, builds large-scale data-analytics and AI platforms for government intelligence agencies and commercial enterprises. Its flagship products are Gotham (for government and defence clients), Foundry (for commercial enterprises), and the Artificial Intelligence Platform (AIP), launched in 2023, which allows organisations to deploy large language models within their existing data infrastructure. The company is headquartered in Denver, Colorado, and is unusual among technology companies in that it derives a substantial share of revenue from classified US government contracts — a relatively insulated revenue stream that also limits disclosure. Palantir built a large retail-investor following due to its association with AI, US defence spending growth, and the outspoken, unconventional public persona of CEO Alex Karp.
ticker_pltr.recent: Palantir's shares reached an all-time high of approximately $207.52 in November 2025, having risen more than 300% from January 2025 on a combination of AI-platform enthusiasm and accelerating commercial revenue growth. The stock suffered a drawdown of roughly 22–38% from that peak through April 2026 — the range reflecting how rapidly sentiment shifted during the broad mega-cap sell-off. As of early May 2026, shares had retraced to around $136, representing a drawdown of more than 34% from the November high.

ticker_lly.description: Eli Lilly is one of the world's largest pharmaceutical companies by market capitalization, transformed in the 2020s by the commercial success of its GLP-1/GIP receptor agonist tirzepatide (Mounjaro for diabetes, Zepbound for obesity). Its next-generation triple agonist retatrutide — targeting GLP-1, GIP, and glucagon receptors simultaneously — produced up to 28.7 percent average body weight loss in Phase 3 TRIUMPH trials and is on track for an NDA filing in late 2026 or early 2027, with potential approval in 2027-2028. Lilly also markets Verzenio (breast cancer), Jardiance (diabetes/heart failure), and Taltz (inflammatory disease).
ticker_lly.blurb: Eli Lilly is one of the world's largest pharmaceutical companies by market capitalization, transformed in the 2020s by the commercial success of its GLP-1/GIP receptor agonist tirzepatide (Mounjaro for diabetes, Zepbound for obesity). Lilly also markets Verzenio (breast cancer), Jardiance (diabetes/heart failure), and Taltz (inflammatory disease).
ticker_lly.recent: Lilly's next-generation triple agonist retatrutide — targeting GLP-1, GIP, and glucagon receptors simultaneously — produced up to 28.7 percent average body weight loss in Phase 3 TRIUMPH trials and is on track for an NDA filing in late 2026 or early 2027, with potential approval in 2027–2028. Trailing-twelve-month revenue is approximately $45 billion against a roughly $700 billion market capitalization in early May 2026.

ticker_tsm.name: Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company
ticker_tsm.blurb: TSMC is the world's largest contract chipmaker, fabricating semiconductors designed by Nvidia, Apple, AMD, Qualcomm, and dozens of others. It controls roughly 60% of global foundry revenue and an even higher share of advanced-node manufacturing (3nm and below). TSMC's competitive position rests on process technology leadership, enormous capital expenditure scale, and a customer base that has no viable alternative at leading-edge geometries. Its Taiwanese concentration is the central geopolitical risk that market participants perpetually discount, then rediscover.
ticker_tsm.recent: TSMC reported Q1 2026 revenue of approximately NT$839 billion (roughly $26 billion USD), up around 41% year-over-year, driven by surging AI accelerator demand from Nvidia and Apple. The company's CoWoS advanced packaging capacity — critical for HBM memory integration in AI GPUs — remains sold out through at least 2026. TSMC appeared on Palantir's Q1 2026 Rule of 80 Frontier chart with a composite growth-plus-margin score of 88%, placing it fourth among large-cap companies on that metric.

poster_felixprehn.blurb: Felix Prehn is a former investment banker turned retail-finance educator and founder of the Goat Academy, a community he describes as aiming to make one million people financially independent. He publishes daily stock-market commentary via podcast, Substack, and X, with a focus on macro-driven equity themes, momentum screening, and accessible explanations of institutional-grade analysis. His style favours pattern-recognition and rules-based frameworks — consistent with a post that distils a CEO's earnings slide into a five-word signal.
poster_felixprehn.credibility_note: Prehn's market commentary is educational rather than licensed investment advice. His background as a former banker is self-reported and not independently verified in public records. Content is broadly accessible and retail-oriented; track record of specific calls is not audited externally.
